title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
official_title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
summary: This is a farm bill — the broad, multi-year law that reauthorizes most U.S. Department of Agriculture programs across twelve subject areas, from crop supports and conservation to food aid, farm credit, rural development, research, forestry, energy, and crop insurance. It also reauthorizes the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, formerly food stamps) and makes administrative changes to how states run it. Many existing program authorizations that lapsed are extended through 2031.
brief: Reauthorizes USDA farm, conservation, trade, rural, research, and crop-insurance programs and SNAP through 2031, with disaster-assistance, specialty-crop, dairy, and SNAP administrative changes.

top_lines.headline: Commodities and Disaster Aid
subs: Extends suspension of permanent price support authority from 2023 to 2031
Creates a Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework for disaster and market losses
Expands the Tree Assistance Program with initial payments and a Sept 30, 2035 sunset

top_lines.headline: SNAP and Nutrition
subs: Lets states hire contractors for SNAP processing when error rates hit 6 percent or backlogs occur
Requires EBT card security rulemaking within 6 months
Makes SNAP online purchasing authority permanent; reauthorizes anti-trafficking enforcement to 2031

top_lines.headline: Conservation, Credit, and Rural Programs
subs: Reauthorizes conservation programs (CRP, EQIP, CSP, easements, partnerships)
Updates farm ownership and operating loan eligibility and limits
Reauthorizes rural development, trade/food-aid, research, forestry, energy, and crop insurance programs

likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Thompson (R-PA), the bill passed the House and was received in the Senate. Comprehensive farm bills typically have bipartisan agricultural-state support, but disagreements over the nutrition title and overall cost can stall reconciliation between the chambers, leaving final passage uncertain.

items.main: Extends commodity price-support authority and adds disaster and specialty-crop assistance.
items.detail: Section 1001 extends the suspension of permanent price support authority under the Agricultural Act of 2014 from 2023 to 2031. Section 1002 expands the Tree Assistance Program — covering biennial crops and pest losses, allowing replanting with alternative varieties, stand densities, or locations, adding a 120-day deadline for application decisions and an optional initial payment, with that payment authority sunsetting September 30, 2035. Section 1003 creates a new Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework for producers hit by adverse events, with payment limits tied to the Food Security Act and a floor of not less than $900,000 for entities deriving at least 75 percent of income from farming. The title also includes dairy reporting, storage facility loans, and supply-chain provisions.

items.main: Reauthorizes SNAP and makes administrative changes to how states operate the program.
items.detail: A new declaration of policy ties SNAP to preventing diet-related chronic disease. Section 4103 lets state agencies hire contractors to handle SNAP certification and other functions when they cannot process applications timely (for reasons such as pandemics, staffing shortages, or disasters), when their payment error rate is at or above 6 percent, or when applications surge — subject to safeguards against incentives to deny eligibility. Other sections make the prohibited-fee provision permanent and extend anti-trafficking and program authorization provisions from 2023 to 2031, require EBT card security rulemaking within 6 months, require reporting of all identified payment errors, and make SNAP online-purchasing authority permanent. Subtitles B and C reauthorize commodity distribution, the commodity supplemental food program, and nutrition-incentive programs.

items.main: Reauthorizes and adjusts USDA conservation programs.
items.detail: The title covers the Conservation Reserve Program and farmable wetland program, the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (including payment limits and conservation innovation grants), the Conservation Stewardship Program with state soil-health assistance, agricultural and forest conservation easement programs, the Regional Conservation Partnership Program, and other programs such as feral swine eradication and emergency conservation and watershed programs. Funding and administration provisions address the Commodity Credit Corporation and delivery of technical assistance.

sections.label: Titles III, V-XII — Trade, Credit, Rural, and Other Programs

items.main: Reauthorizes the remaining farm bill program areas, largely by amending existing USDA statutes.
items.detail: Title III reauthorizes food aid and agricultural trade programs (Food for Peace, McGovern-Dole, Food for Progress, market development). Title V updates farm ownership and operating loan eligibility, experience requirements, and limits. Title VI covers rural development, including rural health and broadband (Rural Electrification Act amendments). Title VII reauthorizes agricultural research, extension, and education. Title VIII addresses forestry, Title IX energy and biofuels, Title X horticulture and marketing, Title XI crop insurance (including a specialty crop advisory committee), and Title XII miscellaneous provisions on livestock and other matters.

underreported.summary: For a person or legal entity that derives at least 75 percent of average gross income from farming, ranching, or silviculture, the standard payment limitation does not apply and the Secretary sets the maximum specialty-crop emergency payment, which may not be set lower than $900,000.
underreported.why_unreported: The framework is presented as broad specialty-crop disaster assistance, but this provision exempts entities deriving at least 75 percent of income from farming from the standard payment limitation and guarantees them a payment ceiling of no less than $900,000, set by the Secretary.

underreported.section: Section 4103 — Contractor Trigger at 6 Percent Error Rate
underreported.summary: States may contract out SNAP certification and other functions whenever their payment error rate reaches 6 percent, in addition to during backlogs or application surges.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision is labeled staffing flexibility, but it also lets a state respond to a high error rate by adding contractors rather than by other corrective measures; the temporary-shortage authority expires only once the error rate falls below 6 percent.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: It is more evident than ever that rural America needs a new farm bill now, not next year or next Congress. Producers are operating under the third consecutive farm bill extension, and the simple truth is the policies of 2018 are no match for the challenges of 2026. It is time to get this critical legislation done. I have said it before and I will say it again, because it is important: This bill was not written in Congress.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Finstad
featured_quotes.text: As a fourth-generation farmer raising that fifth generation, I know firsthand that farm country has faced compounding challenges over the past several years. I am committed to addressing these issues by passing a strong, bipartisan farm bill that is written by farmers and for farmers, by rural communities and for rural communities. The ag title of working families tax cuts made the most significant investment in farm safety net spending since the 2002 farm bill.

gaps: The bill reauthorizes most programs through 2031 but, in the text reviewed, relies on existing statutory funding mechanisms rather than stating new multi-year funding totals for each title.
The bill creates a Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework but makes its payment factor subject to the availability of appropriations without guaranteeing a funding level.
The bill adds SNAP contractor authority tied to error rates and backlogs but does not set standards for contractor accuracy or accountability beyond barring incentives to deny eligibility.
The bill reauthorizes conservation and rural programs but, in the text reviewed, does not specify the enrollment acreage or funding caps for each program in this top-level pass.

added: A Specialty Crop Emergency Assistance Framework (new section 196A) for producers affected by adverse events
SNAP staffing flexibility allowing states to hire contractors during backlogs, surges, or when error rates reach 6 percent
An optional initial-payment option under the Tree Assistance Program, sunsetting September 30, 2035
Permanent authority for SNAP online purchasing

A directive (Section 12306) for the President to have Federal agencies promulgate rules prohibiting purchases of U.S. agricultural land by foreign adversaries, state sponsors of terrorism, and their affiliates
modified: Suspension of permanent price support authority extended from 2023 to 2031
SNAP anti-trafficking enforcement (Sec. 4107) and program appropriations (Sec. 4106) extended from 2023 to 2031; the prohibited-fee provision (Sec. 4102) made permanent

added: Grew from 380 to 456 named sections (~811K to ~992K chars); all 12 titles (Commodities through Miscellaneous) retained, with many sections added within them

New Commodities sections: tobacco restored as an agricultural commodity, dairy business innovation initiatives, electronic forms for disaster assistance, revised livestock-indemnity evidence standards, on-farm fertilizer storage-loan study
New Conservation sections: a Conservation Stewardship Program section (Sec. 2301), conservation activities defined (Sec. 2205), winter-wheat cover-crop study
New animal-welfare sections in Miscellaneous: protection of greyhounds, animal fighting, placement of animals used in federal research
New Sec. 12306 prohibits purchase of agricultural land by foreign entities; new whole-milk-under-the-school-breakfast-program section
New grain-inspection subtitle added (Secs. 12501-12510: declaration of policy, inspection/weighing authority, registration, advisory committee, funding)

New Forestry subtitles added: White Oak Restoration Initiative (Secs. 8601-8606) and Giant Sequoia protection (Secs. 8701-8711), plus Kaibab National Forest restoration, timber-production expansion loan program, Doug LaMalfa Secure Rural Schools Act
New Energy sections: limit on USDA funding for ground-mounted solar, waste-energy recovery added to REAP, tree-planting grant program, second-use battery study
New Nutrition sections: SNAP-eligible hot rotisserie chicken, foods eligible for purchase with SNAP, promoting access to local agriculture
New Trade sections: report on modifications to USMCA, sense of Congress on Argentine beef imports
modified: Several sections renumbered/relabeled (e.g. former Secs. 2301-2302 duties/soil-health shifted to 2302-2303 after the Conservation Stewardship insertion; old 12410-12411 renumbered)

Horticulture organic provisions reworked: pesticide-labeling sections replaced by new organic-integrity definitions, modernized inspection requirements, and National Organic Program oversight study/reform (Secs. 10107-10109)
removed: Dropped pesticide-preemption sections: Uniformity of Pesticide Labeling Requirements, Authority of States, Lawful Use of Authorized Pesticides (former Secs. 10205-10207)
Dropped the Commodity Futures Trading Commission Whistleblower Program section (former Sec. 12409)
Dropped the Office of the Ombudsman section (former Sec. 12206)
